title: LIVE: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
summary: Matt Pocock interviews Dex Horthy - known for the Ralph loop work, formerly of Google, now building Codelayer, an open-source IDE for managing many parallel cloud coding sessions - about making AI coding actually work inside organizations. Dex's thesis: AI can write very good code and best-in-class on brownfield codebases is 2-3x faster for staff-and-above engineers, but only if you know how to hold it, and only if an org standardizes practices, otherwise a hundred good engineers with AI still produce chaos. He explains why his research-plan-implement prompt set grew into a six-step process wrapped in deterministic code: do not use prompts for control flow, use control flow for control flow. On a shared whiteboard they map the smart zone and dumb zone of a context window, quadratic attention, and Ralph as a control loop that advances source (current state) toward specs (desired state) one sized task at a time. Dex tells the war story of a six-hour GCP-VM Ralph that produced a 20,000-line React refactor PR ("Ralph is back") which never merged, versus the pattern that did work: a nightly cron running three iterations so the codebase is a little better every morning. They close with craft that survives the AI era: tracer bullets, learning tests for external SDKs, treating community issues as untrusted input for skip-permissions agents, and reading 20-year-old engineering books because we program in English now.
what_you_learn: This is a field guide to context-window economics, the core constraint of every agent system: why quality degrades quadratically with tokens, how to size loop iterations so edit-test-fix-commit fits in a small context, when to start a fresh context instead of a new message, and why reliable team-wide results come from wrapping prompts in deterministic control flow. The transferable engineering patterns (control loops, tracer bullets, learning tests, untrusted-input gates) apply directly to any agent harness you build or buy.

skills.name: Learning & Teaching
skills.description: Working in the early part of the context window where the model is smartest, and treating roughly 40 percent usage as the paranoia threshold.

skills.name: Context Window Management
skills.description: Every token added to context quadratically increases the compute and attention quality required, so more context means worse results.

skills.name: Context Engineering
skills.description: Managing context deliberately: summarizing state into files, starting fresh contexts, and choosing new context over new messages.

skills.name: AI Output Verification
skills.description: A control loop, like a thermostat, that reads current state and desired state and takes one action to close the gap, forever.

skills.name: Agent Guardrails
skills.description: Deterministic code should orchestrate workflow steps; prompts handle judgment, not sequencing, because control flow is guaranteed to run in order.

skills.name: Task Management
skills.description: Sizing agent tasks so make-change, run-tests, fix, and commit all fit inside one minimal context window.

skills.name: Human-in-the-Loop Collaboration
skills.description: The hardest software problems are solved in collaboration with humans, with agents doing phases and people checking in.

skills.name: Iterative Prototyping
skills.description: One small change that passes through every integration layer first, proving the whole path works before scaling up.

skills.name: Test-Driven Development
skills.description: Unit-style tests, excluded from the normal build, that verify how an external library actually behaves and catch contract changes.

learnings.title: AI can write very good code - if you know how to hold it
learnings.detail: Dex's opening position, quoting Bang from Sourcegraph: you have to know how to hold it. If you have never written code, it is hard to get AI to write good code and hard to know whether the code is good. The target audience is staff and principal engineers at companies with millions of lines and thousands of engineers: best-in-class right now is 2-3x faster on brownfield codebases, plus platforms and practices that standardize how a whole team wields agents - because a hundred engineers all shipping quality code in a hundred different ways still ends in chaos.

learnings.title: From three prompts to six steps: control flow, not prompts, orchestrates
learnings.detail: Six months ago Dex's talk was research-plan-implement: the magic is not in the prompts, there is no perfect prompt, and the words will not stay three steps. Teams that picked up the open-source create plan prompt - about 50 instructions - got great results individually but wildly varying results when handed to their teams. The rebuild wraps the steps in deterministic product code: per 12-factor agents, if you know the workflow, use control flow for control flow because it is guaranteed to run in order; prompts are reserved for the judgment calls, so users no longer need magic words sprinkled at the right moment.

learnings.title: The smart zone and the dumb zone of a context window
learnings.detail: On the whiteboard Dex draws the context window: system message, built-in tools (agents, tasks, read, write, edit), custom MCPs, custom instructions (CLAUDE.md), then user messages, tool calls, and assistant responses. Quality degrades as you fill it because of quadratic attention - attention cost and compute grow with the square of the token count, per layer and per attention head. The practical rule of thumb: around 40 percent context usage is where paranoia should kick in; the exact number flexes by task, but more context always means worse results.

learnings.title: Needle in a haystack benchmarks the wrong thing
learnings.detail: Dex, crediting Geoffrey Huntley, dismisses needle-in-a-haystack long-context benchmarks: real work is not finding one sentence in 100,000 words, it is acting on all 100,000 words - or teasing out the 50,000 that matter - which is a much harder problem the field is still learning to benchmark.

learnings.title: Ask of every message: should this be a new context
learnings.detail: The discipline Dex wants engineered into harnesses: before sending a new message, ask whether it could be a new context instead. Sometimes keeping the context is right - the files are already read, or you lack confidence the model can summarize the session well enough to onboard a fresh window - but the question should always be asked, and ideally the system you design removes the need to ask it.

learnings.title: Ralph is a control loop: current state, desired state, one action
learnings.detail: Dex maps Ralph onto the Kubernetes control-loop idea (a thermostat is the classic example): read the current state of the world, read the desired state, take action, repeat forever. In the Ralph loop the specs are the desired state, the source code is the current state, and each iteration implements exactly one thing, then verifies with tests or a linter. Task sizing is the highest-leverage knob: the task should be small enough to edit, test, fix, and commit within as little context as possible - but not so small that a single signature change can never pass its test in one loop.

learnings.title: The cup is smaller than you think
learnings.detail: Dex's water-and-cups analogy: you have more water than fits in one cup, so you split it across cups - but people underestimate how small the cup is. The agent has less usable context than you think, and you have many levers to manage it: tighten the specs, give better ways to traverse source, rip out custom MCPs, disable built-in tools. If he built a Ralph tool, a core feature would be metrics: chart how much context each loop iteration used and what consumed it, so you can see this loop always hits 60 percent and make the task smaller.

learnings.title: The 20,000-line PR that never merged - and the nightly cron that worked
learnings.detail: Dex's origin story: watching a frontend engineer debug React code, he spent 30 minutes with Claude building a 25-27-rule React style guide (barrel exports or not, useEffect vs Zustand), iterated it with the engineer, then ran a Ralph loop on a GCP VM in tmux with the style guide as desired state and a refactoring plan as the artifact. Six hours later: a 20,000-line, 20-commit PR titled "Ralph is back" - which never merged because two days later it had a hundred merge conflicts. The lesson is not that Ralph failed: killing it cost nothing, and the practical org pattern is a cron running three iterations every night against a standing spec of how the codebase should look, so every morning the codebase is a little better - not a giant PR dumped on coworkers.

learnings.title: Chained Ralphs: specs pipelines and issue triage
learnings.detail: Beyond one loop, Dex describes lispy pipelines of Ralphs: one Ralph reads documentation and extracts clean-room specs, a second asks what the product would look like with more AI, a third turns those specs into working code (he admits his run produced specs he did not love and a product he did not love - part of the game). Matt proposes the simplest possible triage loop: categorize incoming issues, build reproductions, hand them to a second Ralph that fixes and opens PRs. Dex's warning: never feed raw community GitHub issues to an agent in dangerously-skip-permissions mode - issue text is untrusted input with hidden prompts in HTML and markdown. Their own Linear-queue Ralph is gated until a human checks each ticket.

learnings.title: Models cannot plan work the way a human would
learnings.detail: Asked about planning, Dex says the pattern he keeps hitting: models plan in big serial phases (move all 40 things, then wire the API, then refactor the frontend) where a human would move one thing, get the endpoint working, learn from the surprises, then continue. His rule of thumb: how much code would you write before pulling up the web app or pausing to run tests? That is the right task size for Ralph or for a human-on-the-loop plan of five or six steps. Optimize the plan for learning early; segment it the way you would segment your own work.

learnings.title: Tracer bullets: one change through all the layers
learnings.detail: Matt names the concept from The Pragmatic Programmer - Dex realizes he has been teaching exactly this for six months without remembering the name. A tracer bullet is code that goes through every integration layer first so you see that all the layers work, instead of one huge change. The 20-year-old wisdom is more important than ever because it transfers directly to how you prompt and plan agent work.

learnings.title: Read old engineering books - we program in English now
learnings.detail: Matt's sidebar: if you are not reading the classic books, start, because we now program in English and those books are the clearest descriptions of good code ever written - the best prompt-engineering education available. Dex adds learning tests to the list: tests in your unit framework, placed so they do not run on every build, whose job is to verify how an external system actually behaves (for example the Claude Agent SDK, where docs cannot be fully trusted and the code is closed source). Write the assumed contract as assertions and logs; when the vendor later changes session-ID behavior, rerun the test and the contract violation is caught in minutes instead of discovered mid-implementation.

learnings.title: Size phases to verifiable chunks, then check in deliberately
learnings.detail: Dex's closing advice on task size: there is a size that is too small, and the right unit is verifiability - if you can write a unit test for it, do that. For hard work he wants to check in every 100-200 lines, because the worst outcome is 2,000 broken lines with no idea which prompt change would fix it. He designs dual-purpose plans: either one-shot the whole thing while he is away, or - when he has strong opinions - check in after every phase. Either way, every phase is a verifiable chunk, and a growing skill for agent engineers is specifying how the model itself will know the output works as intended.

key_points: Use control flow for control flow - prompts are for judgment, not sequencing.
The cup is smaller than you think: the agent has less usable context than you believe.
Before every message, ask: should this be a new context?
Never send coworkers a 20,000-line refactor PR - run Ralph on a cron, three iterations a night.
Ralph is a lesson in how context windows work, not the final answer for production software.
Needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks are useless; real work means acting on all 100,000 words.
Your instincts as an engineer are still really good - size tasks like you would for yourself.
Community issues are untrusted input for an agent running with skip permissions.
